For example, a cost-benefit analysis could show whether the lighter weight of lithium-sulfur batteries, which are not yet widely available, are worth the initial added cost for deployment in unmanned aerial vehicles. 6.2 Cybersecurity Cyber defense can mitigate risks across the life cycle of digital energy technologies, from procurement, to maintenance, and end of life. For example, implementing cyber-aware practices in procurement processes (e.g., requiring a software bill of materials) can improve supply chain transparency. Employing cyber best practices for all systems would include (1) using a virtual private network for remote connections, (2) employing Transport Layer Security (TLS) for internal networks to encrypt communications between critical assets, (3) deploying a certificate authority for message authentication and secure communications between site equipment, and (4) integrating intrusion detection and protection tools for better alerts on potential threats (Sanghvi et. al. 2021). These measures could collectively improve the security posture of DER systems, reducing the likelihood and impact of cyber threats to DOW’s energy infrastructure. Developing common cyber standards is essential for integrating advanced energy technologies into defense operations while safeguarding against adversarial influence on supply chains. For instance, adhering to the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Special Publication 800 series and the General Services Administration’s as well as Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command’s EV supply equipment guidance when acquiring electrified systems, such as EVs or electric unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), helps mitigate cyber vulnerabilities. Implementing a unified cybersecurity framework early in the development process and 19 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. throughout the charging infrastructure can bolster DOW’s operational system resilience, and standardization helps ensure that the infrastructure remains defensible against potential cyberattacks (Markel and Sanghvi 2022). FERC, in partnership with the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, is also working to enhance supply chain security standards for the power grid, particularly focusing on vulnerabilities in low-impact bulk electric power cyber systems and vendor remote access (FERC 2024; FERC 2025). This work provides a potential model for DOW to consider when coordinating with external utilities or adapting relevant standards for mission-critical systems. Additional mitigations for enhancing cyber resilience in energy systems could include: • Performing cybersecurity risk assessments on DERs: for example, NLR’s Distributed Energy Resource Cybersecurity Framework (DER-CF) tool evaluates the cybersecurity posture of federal sites that employ distributed energy systems or plan to implement DERs for daily operations. The DER-CF helps organizations and federal sites harden their systems against risks by evaluating DER cybersecurity postures and providing customized recommendations for improvement (NLR 2023a) • Collaborating with the newly formed Energy Threat Analysis Center, a DOE-led public- private partnership that convenes experts from the federal government and the U.S. energy sector, to share information regarding threats to energy systems (DOE CESER n.d.) • Using virtual environments, such as the NLR Advanced Research on Integrated Energy Systems (ARIES) Cyber Range, for high-fidelity, at-scale models of a more integrated and interconnected grid to test vulnerabilities, assess shared risks, and explore mitigation strategies
